source.title: Scaling ASR Improves Zero and Few Shot Learning
source.authors: Alex Xiao; Wei-Yi Zheng; Gil Keren; D. Le; Frank Zhang; Christian Fuegen; Ozlem Kalinli; Y. Saraf; Abdel-rahman Mohamed

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling experiments to speech recognition and zero-/few-shot transfer. It reports ASR word error rates, not language-model held-out cross-entropy or fitted power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR WER results across model sizes, data sizes, and transfer settings. These results do not test language-model cross-entropy power laws or compute-optimal allocation. The WER scaling sweep is recorded under fits_no_version; the transfer-task size comparisons bear on V6. The paper also states that 10B results are less consistent and can overfit during fine-tuning.
record.test_reason: The study scales Transformer-transducer ASR models over three encoder sizes (100M, 1B, 10B) and three data sizes, and reports WER. No version applies. V1–V4 and V6 concern language-model pretraining loss or LM downstream tasks, which an ASR transducer is not. V5 requires the same power-law form in another modality, but the paper fits no power law and reports no loss curve. With three sizes and non-monotonic WER, the power-law form cannot be read. The study cites Kaplan only to motivate scaling data and model together. Its findings on WER versus model and data size are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that scaling model and data together improves universal ASR, and that zero- and few-shot transfer benefits from going from 100M to 1B. 10B transfer results are less consistent and point to overfitting. They also stress data quality and diversity, including length diversity, over quantity.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales Transformer-transducer ASR models and reports WER, rather than fitting held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The benefit of increasing model size depends on training-data size; 10B transfer results vary by domain and video length, and fine-tuning can overfit.

fits_no_version.finding: For ASR WER, going from 1B to 10B parameters helps only at the largest data size. Average relative WER changes are +7.32%, +2.19% and -4.03% at 13K, 130K and 1.3M hours. Going from 130K to 1.3M hours helps the 10B model by 8.46% but the 100M model by only 0.01%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ASR, gains from parameter scaling depend on data size, and model and data must grow together for larger models to help.

fits_no_version.finding: In zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer, 100M to 1B generally improves WER. 10B is inconsistent: worse on AphasiaBank and long videos, best on short videos. The 10B model also overfits in ultra-low-resource SPGISpeech fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transfer performance of ASR models does not improve monotonically with parameter count beyond about 1B.

fits_no_version.finding: Filtering 3.2M hours down to 1.3M hours keeps overall WER about the same and improves rare-word WER by 4–6% relative (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ASR, data quality and diversity can matter more than raw data quantity.

record.problems: The paper reports WER rather than held-out cross-entropy and does not fit or test power laws. Several plotted scaling results are given as relative changes rather than full numerical results in the text. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 includes additional model-size and domain results, including SPGISpeech adaptation settings. They were not separately extracted because the flattened table layout in the supplied text does not unambiguously assign all values to the relevant columns.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or loss curve for speech. Only three model sizes and three data sizes, reported as WER.
No language-model downstream tasks. The ASR transfer comparisons involve no LM and no prediction from scale or loss.
Shape is varied together with size, never at a fixed parameter count.

missing.what: SPGISpeech results by model size and fine-tuning data amount (5000h to 10m). The text says 1B beats 100M by 13% to 23% relative, while 10B overfits in ultra-low-resource settings.
Data-size scaling at fixed model size: 130K to 1.3M hours improves the 100M, 1B and 10B models by 0.01%, 1.67% and 8.46% relative.

record.verdict_notes: ASR scaling study with no loss curves or power-law fits. The reader's V6 links are dropped because ASR transducers are not language models. Its labels are removed. Rows r3 and r4 report Fold 1 values mislabeled as AphasiaBank Overall.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or power-law fit is reported.
No small-run power-law extrapolation is tested against larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count is reported.
The paper studies speech ASR and transfer, but does not test whether held-out loss follows the same power-law form in another modality or training regime.
Tests ASR transfer performance at selected model sizes and domains, not broad downstream-task predictability from pretraining loss or fitted scaling laws.
No fitted exponents, alternative fitting choices, or departures from a single power-law curve are analyzed.
